opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that there isn't a single magic number yet, but I can share how I think about it.

If you look at language models, the breakthroughs came when we reached the trillions of tokens. Embodied data is very different. A single hour of robot interaction carries much richer information than an hour of text: vision, depth, proprioception, force, and the consequences of actions. So comparing on raw token counts can be misleading.

My intuition is that for a truly embodied-native foundation model, one trained from the start on embodied data rather than a vision-language model with an action head attached, you probably need somewhere on the order of millions of hours of high-quality interaction data. Today the whole field combined has maybe tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand hours, depending on how you count. So we're still one or two orders of magnitude short.

But scale alone isn't the point. Three things matter as much as volume.

The first is diversity. Ten thousand hours of the same arm picking up the same cup in the same lab is worth much less than a thousand hours across many homes, objects, lighting conditions, and failure cases. Failures especially are underrated. The model needs to see what goes wrong and how to recover.

The second is the data pyramid. I see it in layers: a huge base of human video and egocentric data that's cheap and abundant, a middle layer of simulation and synthetic data, and a smaller but very precious top layer of real robot teleoperation and autonomous rollouts. The ideal scale differs for each layer. The base might be billions of clips, while the top might only need hundreds of thousands of hours if it's well curated.

The third is the closed loop. Once robots are deployed and collecting their own data, the question changes from "how much data do we need" to "how fast can the flywheel spin." That's really what happened with autonomous driving. The companies that won weren't the ones with the biggest initial dataset but the ones whose fleets kept generating useful data.

So if you push me for a number, I'd say a million hours of diverse real-world embodied interaction is roughly where I'd expect to see emergent generalization, something like a GPT-3 moment for robotics. But I'd also bet the path there runs through better data efficiency and the right mix of sources, not just brute-force collection.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates about one million hours for emergent generalization, but does not frame that amount as balancing embodied data with internet data in the overall model.

r002.rationale: The candidate says an embodied-native model likely needs millions of hours. It does not propose 100,000 hours for pretraining without starting from a digital model.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "ideal data scale" is a slightly misleading way to frame it, because the number only makes sense relative to what kind of data you're talking about and what the model is supposed to do with it.

Let me give a rough picture of how I think about it. When people say "scale" in the LLM world, they mean tokens, tens of trillions of them, scraped from the internet. For embodied intelligence, there is no equivalent internet. Nobody has been quietly recording billions of hours of robots doing things. So if you set your target as "the same scale as language," you've basically defined an impossible goal, and then you spend all your time on collection and none on figuring out what the model actually needs.

So I prefer to think in layers. At the bottom you have massive video and image data from the internet, which is essentially free and basically unlimited. That data teaches the model about physics, object permanence, how things look when they move, how hands interact with objects. It doesn't carry actions, but it carries a lot of world structure, and I think a lot of the "common sense" of an embodied model should come from there. The next layer is human egocentric or demonstration video, which is much smaller but much closer to what a robot needs: intent, manipulation strategies, task structure. And the top layer is real robot data with actions and proprioception, which is the most expensive and the smallest.

If you force me to put numbers on it: internet-scale video, essentially as much as you can process; something on the order of millions of hours of human-centric video; and for real robot data, I think we'll see a meaningful phase change somewhere in the range of tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand hours, provided the diversity is right. I want to stress that last condition. Ten thousand hours of one robot picking up the same cup in the same lab is almost worthless compared to a thousand hours spread across many embodiments, many scenes, many tasks. Diversity is the actual bottleneck, not raw hours.

And then there's simulation and synthetic data, which I think people underrate on one side and overhype on the other. It's not going to replace real data, but it's extremely good at filling the long tail, especially for things that are rare or dangerous to collect in the real world. So the honest answer is: the ideal scale is whatever amount lets you cover the distribution of situations you care about densely enough that the model stops memorizing and starts generalizing. For language that happened to be trillions of tokens. For embodiment I don't think the number will be that large, because the real-world signal per sample is much richer, but the cost per sample is also much higher, so we have to be far more deliberate about what we collect.

r001.rationale: The response describes internet-scale video, millions of hours of human-centric video, and tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand hours of robot data. It does not identify roughly one million hours of embodied data as a balance point with internet data.

r002.rationale: It gives a robot-data range that could include 100,000 hours, but does not propose that scale for embodied-native pretraining without starting from a digital model.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think there’s a single ideal number yet. For an embodied-native foundation model, data scale has to mean more than hours of video or the number of robot trajectories. It also matters how many environments, tasks, objects, and types of interaction the model experiences.

You could collect a huge amount of data repeating the same action in the same setting, and still get a model that struggles when something changes. I’d want data that connects perception, action, and consequences, including failures and recovery, across diverse situations.

So I would work backward from generalization: can the model handle a new task or environment with very little additional experience? Then I’d increase both the volume and diversity of training data and measure how that ability improves. Without that evidence, naming a particular data scale would be premature.

r001.rationale: The candidate says no single ideal number is established and does not identify roughly one million hours or a balance with internet data.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not propose 100,000 hours or discuss pretraining without starting from a digital model.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t define the ideal scale by a single number of hours or trajectories. For an embodied-native foundation model, the key is how much meaningful interaction the data captures: different environments, tasks, objects, and actions, and the consequences of those actions.

A large dataset of repetitive successful demonstrations may teach less than a smaller dataset that includes diverse situations, failures, and recovery. The model needs to learn how its actions change the world, not just what the world looks like.

So I would think about scale in terms of coverage and generalization. As we add data, can the model handle new tasks and unfamiliar environments with less additional training? That’s the signal I’d use to judge whether we’re reaching the right scale, rather than committing to a particular number upfront.

r001.rationale: The response rejects a single numerical scale and gives no threshold of roughly one million hours or balance with internet data.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose 100,000 hours for embodied-native pretraining or address pretraining without a digital model.
